title: AI Productivity Systems
subtitle: Build measured, repeatable AI routines for your own work and your team, and prove the time they save.
description: Move from occasional chatbot use to a deliberate system: mapped tasks, a reusable context store, routine cards with review gates, and a work log that shows what really saves time. You then learn to run discovery, price coaching work and lead a team to adopt the same system, ending with a measured case study.
outcomes: Break recurring work into steps and decide which steps AI, templates or you should handle
Build a context store and routine cards that produce reliable first drafts every week
Run a review gate and an AI work log, and decide with your own figures which routines to keep
Run discovery with a team and price a scoped build-and-coach engagement
Lead team adoption with a shared playbook and present an honest portfolio case study
audience: Professionals, team leads, small business owners and aspiring coaches who already use AI tools and want consistent, measurable results from them.
tools: A smartphone or laptop with internet access
One AI assistant account (for example ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini; free plans are enough to start)
A cloud documents and spreadsheet tool such as Google Docs and Sheets
A phone stopwatch for timing tasks

modules.title: Foundations: From Prompts to a Working System
modules.overview: This module moves you from occasional AI use to a deliberate system. You learn the five parts every AI productivity system needs, how to break recurring work into steps and decide who does each step, and how to build the context store that makes an AI assistant genuinely useful for your work.

lessons.title: From one-off prompts to a working system: the five parts
objectives: Explain the difference between occasional AI use and an AI productivity system
Name the five parts of a system: capture, context, routines, review gate and log
Estimate the weekly time a system saves, including the time spent checking
Work out how quickly the setup time pays for itself

blocks.text: Most people use AI the way they use a calculator found on a table: when they remember it is there. They open a chatbot, type a quick question, copy the answer and move on. Next week they start again from nothing, explaining their organisation, their audience and their style all over again. The results are uneven, and the time saved is small and hard to see.

An **AI productivity system** is different. It is a small set of habits, files and checks that make AI part of how your recurring work gets done, every week, whether or not you feel inspired. The AI tool is only one piece. The system is what you build around it so that good results come out reliably and mistakes are caught before anyone else sees them.

blocks.name: online-organizer
blocks.alt: A woman arranging tasks and notes on a large screen organiser
blocks.caption: A system organises the work around the AI tool, not just the tool itself.

blocks.text: The five parts of every system

head: Part
What it does
What it looks like on a phone
rows: 1. Capture
Collects raw material in one place: ideas, requests, notes, voice notes
One notes app or one WhatsApp chat with yourself where everything lands
2. Context store
Holds what the AI needs to know about you and your work
A context file, templates, past good examples and a facts sheet
3. Routines
Turns recurring tasks into repeatable steps with a fixed trigger
A routine card: every Monday at 8am, draft the weekly announcement
4. Review gate
Checks AI output before it leaves your hands
A short checklist: names, numbers, dates, private data, tone
5. Log and improve
Records what each routine cost and saved, so you can fix or drop it
A simple sheet with one line per routine run

blocks.title: How the five parts work together
items: Capture raw material
Add saved context
Run the routine
Check at the gate
Log and improve
blocks.caption: Each run of a routine feeds the log, and the log tells you how to improve the context and the routine next time.

blocks.text: Notice what is missing from the list: there is no part called "find the best AI app". Tools change often and new features appear every few months. A system built on clear routines and a good context store can move from one tool to another in an afternoon. A habit of random prompting cannot be moved, because there is nothing written down to move.
What a system is not

items: **Not more apps.** A good system often uses fewer tools than before: one place to capture, one assistant, one home for files.
**Not automation without a human.** In this course every routine has a review gate. You decide what leaves your hands.
**Not AI everywhere.** Some tasks are faster done by hand, and some must never pass through an AI tool, such as private member records or money approvals.
**Not a one-day project.** You build it in small pieces and keep only what proves useful in your log.

blocks.title: Worked example: a coordinator's week before and after a system
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi coordinates volunteers for a women's network in Enugu. She has three weekly tasks and one monthly report. She timed each task for two weeks before building anything, then timed them again after setting up routines. All times include her checking and editing.
steps: Monday announcement to the WhatsApp group: 40 minutes before, 15 minutes after (a saved prompt plus her context file gives a first draft she edits).
Answering repeat questions from members (venue, dues, dates): 60 minutes before, 30 minutes after (a facts sheet in her context store lets the AI draft replies she checks and sends).
Volunteer roster message: 30 minutes before, 12 minutes after (a template and a routine card).
Weekly total: 40 + 60 + 30 = 130 minutes before; 15 + 30 + 12 = 57 minutes after. She saves 73 minutes a week.
Monthly report: 180 minutes before, 90 minutes after. Over a four-week month she saves 73 x 4 = 292 minutes on weekly tasks plus 90 on the report, 382 minutes in all, a little over 6 hours.
Setup took her about 3 hours (180 minutes) spread over one weekend. At 73 minutes a week, 180 / 73 is about 2.5, so the weekly routines alone repaid the setup in under three weeks.
blocks.result: Ngozi gets back roughly six hours a month, and she can show the numbers because she timed the work before and after. Without the before figures, she would only have a feeling that things were faster.

blocks.title: Time it before you change it
blocks.text: Before you build any routine, time the task the old way at least twice. Use your phone's stopwatch and write the minutes in a note. Your own before-and-after figures are the only honest proof that the system works for you.
Why systems beat occasional use

Three things improve when AI use becomes a system. First, **quality becomes consistent**, because every run uses the same tested prompt and the same context, so you are not relying on how well you happened to phrase a question that day. Second, **checking becomes faster**, because you learn exactly where this routine tends to go wrong and you look there first. Third, **improvement compounds**: each time you fix a prompt or add a fact to your context store, every future run benefits.

The rest of this course builds each part in turn. In this module you map your work and build your context store. In Module 2 you choose tools, write routine cards and set up your review gate and log. In Module 3 you learn to help a team or a paying client build the same thing, and to present your own results as evidence.

blocks.title: Saved time is only real if quality holds
blocks.text: If a routine saves 20 minutes but sends out a wrong date that you then spend an hour correcting, it has cost you time. That is why the review gate and the log are part of the system, not optional extras.

takeaways: A system is habits, files and checks around an AI tool, not the tool itself.
The five parts are capture, context store, routines, review gate, and log and improve.
Count checking and editing time when you measure what a routine saves.
Time a task the old way before you change it, so you have honest before-and-after figures.

activity.title: Time three recurring tasks
steps: List three tasks you do every week or every month, in your own words.
Next time you do each one, time it with your phone stopwatch from start to finish.
Write the minutes, the date and what slowed you down in a note.
Mark which of the five parts is missing for each task (for example, no saved context or no template).
activity.evidence: A note or photo of your three task timings with the missing part marked for each.

lessons.title: Breaking recurring work into steps and assigning each step
objectives: Build a two-week inventory of recurring tasks with frequency and minutes
Break a task into its steps and assign each step one of four roles
Use a frequency and judgement map to decide which tasks to build routines for first
Calculate the monthly minutes a redesigned task saves

blocks.text: The most common mistake in AI productivity is asking, "Can AI do this task?" The honest answer is usually "partly". A monthly report, a parents' update or a funding application is not one action. It is a chain of steps: gathering information, deciding what matters, writing, checking facts, formatting and sending. AI is strong at some of those steps and weak or risky at others. Systems are built at the level of **steps**, not whole tasks.

blocks.name: task-list
blocks.alt: A person ticking items on a long task list
blocks.caption: Your recurring task list is the raw material of your system.

blocks.text: Step 1: a two-week recurring task inventory

For two ordinary weeks, keep a simple list of every task you do more than once a month. For each one, write how often it happens and roughly how many minutes it takes. Then multiply to get **minutes per month**. A 15-minute task done every working day (about 22 times a month) costs 330 minutes a month, far more than a 2-hour task done once a month. This simple multiplication often changes what you think your biggest time costs are.
Step 2: break the task into steps and assign roles
Take your largest task and write its steps in order, as if teaching a new assistant. Then give each step one of four roles.

head: Role
Meaning
Typical steps
rows: Me only
Needs your judgement, relationships, authority or access to private data
Deciding priorities, approving money, writing about a sensitive matter, handling member records
AI drafts, I edit
AI produces a first version from your notes and context; you correct and own it
Turning bullet notes into a message, a report section or a plain-language summary
AI checks, I decide
You write; AI reviews for gaps, clarity or tone; you choose what to accept
Proofreading, checking a draft against a checklist, suggesting a simpler wording
Tool or template
No AI needed: a formula, saved template or checklist does it better
Totals and counts in a spreadsheet, a fixed message layout, a form

blocks.title: Never give AI the sums
blocks.text: Chat assistants can make arithmetic and counting mistakes while sounding confident. Totals, balances and counts belong in a spreadsheet formula such as SUM or COUNTIF, which you can check. Give the AI the finished figures to write about, not the job of calculating them.

blocks.title: Worked example: redesigning a monthly parents' update
blocks.context: For example, Amaka runs a tailoring training centre in Aba with 24 learners. Every month she sends each learner's parent or sponsor a short progress message on WhatsApp. She timed the task the old way and then redesigned it step by step.
steps: Compile attendance from the paper register: 40 minutes. New role: Tool or template. She enters attendance in a sheet with a COUNTIF formula: 10 minutes.
Write a progress note per learner (skills learned, what to practise): 24 x 2 = 48 minutes. Role: Me only, because it needs her judgement. Still 48 minutes.

Write 24 personalised messages: 24 x 4 = 96 minutes. New role: AI drafts, I edit. She pastes her notes (first names only) in batches with a saved prompt: 20 minutes, plus 1 minute checking each message, 24 minutes. New total 44 minutes.
Add fee balances from her ledger: 20 minutes. Role: Me only. Balances are typed in by her after the draft and never pasted into the AI. Still 20 minutes.
Proofread and check tone: 15 minutes. New role: AI checks, I decide: 8 minutes.
Send on WhatsApp: 30 minutes. Role: Me only. Still 30 minutes.
blocks.result: Amaka saves 89 minutes a month, about 36 percent. Half of her steps did not change at all, and one of the biggest savings came from a spreadsheet formula, not from AI. That is a normal, healthy result.

blocks.text: Step 3: decide where to start

You cannot redesign everything at once. Place each task on a simple map using two questions: how often does it repeat, and how much judgement does it need? Tasks that repeat often and need little judgement are your best first routines, because each improvement pays back many times and mistakes are easy to spot.

blocks.title: Frequency and judgement map
items: Do it yourself, carefully
AI prepares, you decide
Occasional AI help
Build a routine first
axes: How often it repeats (low to high)
How much judgement it needs (low to high)
blocks.caption: Start with frequent, low-judgement tasks; keep rare, high-judgement tasks in your own hands.

items: **Build a routine first (frequent, low judgement):** weekly announcements, roster messages, standard replies.
**AI prepares, you decide (frequent, high judgement):** weekly priorities, responses to complaints. AI can gather and draft; you make the call.
**Occasional AI help (rare, low judgement):** a one-off flyer text or a list of ideas. Use AI when needed, no routine required.
**Do it yourself, carefully (rare, high judgement):** a letter to a funder, a staff disciplinary matter, anything legal or financial.

blocks.title: Some tasks should simply stop
blocks.text: While mapping, you will find tasks that nobody reads or needs, such as a report that duplicates another one. Removing a task saves more time than any AI routine. Ask the person who receives it before you stop, and record the decision.

takeaways: Design systems at the level of steps, not whole tasks.
Minutes per month (frequency x minutes) shows your true time costs.
Use four roles: Me only, AI drafts and I edit, AI checks and I decide, Tool or template.
Calculations belong in spreadsheet formulas, not in a chat assistant.
Start with tasks that repeat often and need little judgement.

activity.title: Redesign one recurring task
steps: Keep a recurring task inventory for two weeks and calculate minutes per month for each task.
Choose the task with the highest minutes per month that does not involve private records or money approvals.
Write its steps in order and give each step one of the four roles.
Estimate the new minutes for each step and add up before and after totals.
activity.evidence: Your inventory and a step table for one task showing roles and before-and-after minutes.

lessons.title: Your context store: context file, templates, examples and facts
objectives: Write a personal context file that fits the space your AI tool allows
Build the four layers of a context store: context file, templates, examples and reference facts
Choose where to keep context in ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or NotebookLM, plus an offline copy
Keep private and personal data out of your context store

blocks.text: An AI assistant knows a great deal about the world but nothing about you. It does not know your organisation's name, who your members are, which words your leader dislikes, or that your audience reads on small phones with costly data. If you leave that out, you get a generic answer and spend your time fixing it. If you supply it every time by typing, you waste time. The answer is a **context store**: written material you prepare once and reuse in every routine.

blocks.name: personal-notebook
blocks.alt: A person writing in a personal notebook beside a laptop
blocks.caption: Your context store is written once and reused in every routine.

blocks.text: The four layers of a context store

blocks.title: Layers of a context store
items: Context file: who and how
Templates: shape of outputs
Examples: what good looks like
Reference facts: checked details
blocks.caption: The short context file sits on top; the larger layers below are attached only when a routine needs them.

items: **Context file:** a short description of your role, organisation, audiences, tone, words to use or avoid, and preferred formats. It goes into every conversation.
**Templates:** the fixed shape of recurring outputs, such as the headings of a monthly report or the layout of a weekly announcement.
**Examples:** two or three past outputs you were proud of. Showing the AI a good example is often more effective than describing one.
**Reference facts:** a dated facts sheet with correct names, titles, venues, dates, prices and programme details. Update it when anything changes, and write the date of the last update at the top.

blocks.text: Where to keep it in common tools

The main assistants now have a place to store context so you do not paste it every time. Features and limits change, so check the help pages listed in this course's sources before relying on a detail.

head: Tool
Where context goes
Points to know
rows: ChatGPT
Custom instructions (applies to all chats) and Projects (chats, files and instructions kept together)
OpenAI's help page gives custom instructions up to 1,500 characters on Free and Go plans and up to 5,000 on paid plans; free Projects hold up to 5 files
Claude
Projects, with project knowledge (uploaded documents) and project instructions
Anthropic's help page says free accounts can create up to five projects
Gemini
Gems: saved instructions plus knowledge files from your device or Google Drive
Google says Gems on personal accounts are moving to a feature called skills from November 2026
NotebookLM
A notebook of your own sources: PDFs, websites, Google Docs, Slides, audio
Answers include in-line citations to your sources, which makes it suited to research routines

blocks.text: Always keep a master copy of your context store outside any AI tool, for example in a Google Docs folder or your phone's notes, saved for offline use. If you change tools, lose access to an account or your plan changes, you paste it into the new tool and carry on.

blocks.title: Worked example: fitting a context file into 1,500 characters
blocks.context: For example, Halima is communications lead for a women's cooperative network in Kano and uses the free ChatGPT plan, where custom instructions allow up to 1,500 characters. Her first draft context file is too long. She counts characters in Google Docs using Tools, then Word count.
steps: Her draft has six sections: role 310 characters, audiences 420, tone 380, words to avoid 260, formats 450, organisation history 520.
Total: 310 + 420 + 380 + 260 + 450 + 520 = 2,340 characters, which is 840 over the limit.
She moves the organisation history (520) out of the context file and into a reference document in a Project, because it is only needed for some tasks.
She shortens formats from 450 to 250 (minus 200) by keeping only her two most used formats, and audiences from 420 to 220 (minus 200) by cutting repeated description.
New total: 2,340 minus 520 minus 200 minus 200 = 1,420 characters, leaving 80 characters of spare room.
blocks.result: Halima's context file now fits the free limit and applies to every chat, while the longer history sits in a reference file used only when a routine needs it. Her first drafts now open with the network's correct name and tone without any extra typing.

blocks.text: A context file outline you can copy

items: Role: "I am the [role] at [organisation], a [type] in [city/country]."
Audiences: who reads your work and what they need, for example "members on phones, many with limited data; prefer short paragraphs".
Tone: three adjectives and one sentence of guidance, for example "warm, respectful, direct; address members as 'dear members'".
Words: terms to use (official programme names) and to avoid (jargon, slang, words your leader dislikes).
Formats: your two or three most common outputs and their length limits.
Working rules: "If information is missing, ask me rather than guessing. Never invent figures, names or dates."

blocks.title: What never goes into a context store
blocks.text: Keep out phone numbers, home addresses, health details, bank or BVN numbers, ID numbers, passwords and anything a member told you in confidence. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023, enforced by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, gives people rights over their personal data, so use first names or roles in examples and keep personal records in your own protected files.
Keeping the store alive

A context store slowly goes stale: a venue changes, a programme is renamed, a new leader prefers a different greeting. Put a recurring reminder in your calendar for the first working day of each month to read your facts sheet and context file and update anything that has changed. Write the update date at the top. An out-of-date facts sheet is dangerous, because the AI will repeat old details with full confidence.

takeaways: A context store has four layers: context file, templates, examples and reference facts.
Check your tool's limits; ChatGPT free custom instructions allow up to 1,500 characters.
Move long background material into project files and keep the context file short.
Keep a master copy outside any AI tool and review it monthly.
Personal and confidential data never goes into the store.

activity.title: Build your context store
steps: Write your context file using the six-part outline and count its characters.
Trim or move material until it fits the limit of the tool you use.
Collect one template and two good past examples for your top recurring task.
Create a dated facts sheet with the names, dates and details your routines need.
Load the context file into your tool and save a master copy in a folder you can open offline.
activity.evidence: Your context file with its character count, plus a screenshot of the folder holding your template, examples and facts sheet.

quiz.q: Ngozi's weekly tasks took 130 minutes before her system and 57 minutes after, including checking. Setup took 180 minutes. Roughly how many weeks until the setup pays for itself?
options: About 1 week
About 2.5 weeks
About 6 weeks
It never pays back
quiz.explain: She saves 130 minus 57, which is 73 minutes a week. 180 divided by 73 is about 2.5, so the setup is repaid in under three weeks.

quiz.q: Which of these is part of an AI productivity system as taught in this course?
options: Finding the newest AI app each month
Letting AI send messages without anyone checking
A review gate that checks names, numbers and private data before output leaves you
Using AI for every task to save the most time
quiz.explain: The five parts are capture, context store, routines, review gate, and log and improve. A review gate is essential; the other options describe habits the course warns against.

quiz.q: Amaka needs the number of classes each learner attended this month. Which role should this step get?
options: Tool or template: a spreadsheet COUNTIF formula
AI drafts, I edit
AI checks, I decide
Me only, counted by hand each time
quiz.explain: Counts and totals belong in a spreadsheet formula, which is reliable and checkable. Chat assistants can make counting mistakes while sounding confident.

quiz.q: A task repeats every week and needs little judgement, such as a standard roster message. Where does it sit on the frequency and judgement map?
options: Do it yourself, carefully
Occasional AI help
AI prepares, you decide
Build a routine first
quiz.explain: Frequent, low-judgement tasks are the best first routines because each improvement pays back often and errors are easy to spot.

quiz.q: Halima's context file is 2,340 characters but her plan allows 1,500. What is the best fix?
options: Paste it in two halves so the tool reads both
Move long background material into a project reference file and shorten repeated sections
Delete the working rule about not inventing figures
Switch off custom instructions and type context each time
quiz.explain: Keep the always-on context file short and move material only some tasks need into reference files. The rule against invented figures is one of the most important lines to keep.

quiz.q: Which item should NEVER go into a context store?
options: The organisation's official programme names
A list of words the leader prefers to avoid
Members' phone numbers and health details
Two past announcements that worked well
quiz.explain: Personal data such as phone numbers and health details stays out of AI tools. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 gives people rights over their personal data.

modules.title: Tools, Routines and Quality Control
modules.overview: This module turns your map and context store into working routines. You choose a lean tool stack that suits your phone, data budget and privacy needs, write routine cards for recurring tasks, and set up the review gate, work log and fallback plan that keep the system honest and reliable.

lessons.title: Choosing a lean, low-data AI stack and setting it up safely
objectives: Describe the four layers of a personal AI stack
Compare stack options with a weighted scoring table
Reduce data costs when using AI tools on a phone
Complete a safety setup checklist for your accounts

blocks.text: A productivity system needs tools, but fewer than most people think. Every extra app is another password, another place where notes get lost, and more data used to sync. The goal is a **lean stack**: one tool for each job, chosen for how you actually work, on the phone or laptop you actually have.

blocks.name: mobile-phone
blocks.caption: For many learners the whole stack runs on one phone, so every tool must earn its place.

blocks.text: The four layers of a personal stack

head: Layer
Job
Common choices
rows: Capture
Catch ideas, requests and notes the moment they arrive
Phone notes app, Google Keep, a WhatsApp chat with yourself, voice notes
Assistant
Draft, summarise, check and research with your saved context
ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, NotebookLM for source-based research
Home for files
Keep the context store, templates, routine cards and finished work
Google Drive and Docs, OneDrive, a single folder on your laptop
Calendar and reminders
Fire each routine at the right time
Google Calendar, phone reminders, a printed weekly sheet

blocks.text: Pick one choice per layer and stay with it for at least a month before judging it. Changing tools every week means you never build the habit, and the habit is what produces results. If your organisation already uses Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, starting inside what you already pay for and know is usually wiser than adding a new platform.
Comparing options with a weighted score

When you have two or three realistic options, do not choose by excitement. List what matters, give each criterion a weight that adds up to 100, score each option from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent), multiply and add. The scores are your own judgements after trying each option for a few days.

blocks.title: Worked example: scoring three stack options
blocks.context: For example, Chioma runs a small events business in Port Harcourt from her phone. She tried three stacks for one week each and wrote her own scores. Weights: works well on her phone 30, data use 25, free plan covers her needs 20, easy to share with her assistant 15, privacy controls she understands 10.
steps: Stack A (a chat assistant app plus her phone notes app) scored 5, 3, 4, 2, 4. Weighted: 150 + 75 + 80 + 30 + 40 = 375, so 3.75 out of 5.
Stack B (an assistant from the same company as the email and cloud documents she already uses) scored 4, 4, 4, 4, 3. Weighted: 120 + 100 + 80 + 60 + 30 = 390, so 3.90.
Stack C (a team workspace app with built-in AI) scored 3, 4, 3, 5, 4. Weighted: 90 + 100 + 60 + 75 + 40 = 365, so 3.65.
She checks the result against her gut feeling. Stack C shares best, but sharing only carries 15 points for a business of two people.
blocks.result: Stack B wins with 3.90, mainly because it shares easily with her assistant and keeps files where they already are. If Chioma hires more staff, the sharing weight would rise and Stack C might win, so she notes to re-score in six months.

blocks.text: Keeping data costs down

items: **Prefer text.** Typed chats use far less data than voice conversations, image generation or video.
**Upload big files on Wi-Fi.** Large PDFs and recordings for a Project or NotebookLM are best added when you have cheaper or free Wi-Fi access, not on mobile data.
**Make documents available offline.** Google Docs and Drive allow offline access on phones, so you can read and edit your context store and templates without data.
**Turn off auto-download** of media in WhatsApp for groups you only need to read.
**Batch your AI work.** Running three routines in one session uses less data and attention than opening the app ten times a day.

blocks.text: Safety setup before you start

blocks.title: Account safety setup
items: Unique strong password
Two-step verification switched on
Chat data settings reviewed
Phone screen lock enabled
Offline master copy saved
blocks.caption: Complete all five before you load your context store into any tool.

blocks.text: Each assistant has privacy or data controls in its settings, including options about whether your chats may be used to improve the company's models and how long chat history is kept. Open the settings, read each option and choose deliberately. Settings and their names change, so check the official help pages rather than relying on a friend's description.

blocks.title: Scam warning
blocks.text: Fraudsters advertise fake "AI apps", fake premium accounts and "cheap shared logins" on social media and WhatsApp. Install assistant apps only from the official Google Play Store or Apple App Store listing under the real company name, pay for subscriptions only inside the official app or website, and never share your login or one-time codes with anyone.

blocks.title: Work accounts and personal accounts
blocks.text: If your employer gives you an approved AI tool, use it for work data and keep your personal account for personal tasks. Ask your manager or IT lead which tools are approved before putting any work documents into an AI service.

takeaways: A lean stack has one tool per layer: capture, assistant, home for files, calendar.
Use a weighted score with your own ratings to choose between realistic options.
Text chats, Wi-Fi uploads and offline documents keep data costs down.
Complete the safety checklist before loading your context store into any tool.

activity.title: Choose and secure your stack
steps: Write your current tool for each of the four layers, and cross out any duplicates.
If you are deciding between options, try each for a few days and fill in a weighted score table.
Complete the five-item safety checklist for your chosen assistant account.
Make your context store folder available offline on your phone.
activity.evidence: Your stack list (and score table if used) plus a tick list showing the five safety items completed.

lessons.title: Routine cards: turning recurring work into repeatable AI workflows
objectives: Write a routine card with trigger, inputs, saved prompt, check, output and time box
Keep calculations and private data outside the AI step of a routine
Design a research routine that checks every key fact against an official source
Run a routine for the first time and record how it went

blocks.text: A good intention such as "I will use AI for my reports" fades within weeks. A **routine card** does not, because it answers every practical question in advance: when it happens, what you gather, which saved prompt you run, what you check and where the result goes. It is a one-page recipe for one recurring task. When you are tired or busy, you follow the card instead of thinking from scratch.

blocks.name: schedule
blocks.alt: A person arranging tasks on a weekly calendar
blocks.caption: Each routine card has a fixed trigger on your calendar, so it happens even in a busy week.

blocks.text: The parts of a routine card

head: Field
What to write
Example
rows: Name
Short and specific
Monthly savings group update
Trigger
A fixed time or event
Last Friday of the month, 7pm, after collections close
Inputs
Exactly what you gather first
Totals from the contributions sheet; list of next month's dates
Saved prompt
Where the tested prompt is stored
Prompt library, item 4, in Drive
Check
What you verify before sending
Totals match the sheet; no names of owing members; dates match the facts sheet
Output
What is produced and where it goes
One WhatsApp group message; private reminders sent one by one
Time box
The minutes you allow
20 minutes
Log
What you record afterwards
Minutes taken, edits needed, errors caught

blocks.title: One run of a routine
items: Trigger fires
Gather inputs
Run saved prompt
Check against sources
Send and log
blocks.caption: The AI works only in the middle step; you own the inputs, the check and the delivery.

blocks.title: Worked example: a monthly savings group update
blocks.context: For example, Funmi is treasurer of a 30-member rotating savings group (ajo) in Ibadan. Each member contributes 5,000 naira a month. She keeps contributions in a Google Sheet and used to spend about an hour writing the monthly update.
steps: Inputs: the sheet totals expected contributions with a formula: 30 x 5,000 = 150,000 naira. It shows 26 members paid in full (130,000 naira), 2 paid half (2 x 2,500 = 5,000 naira) and 2 have not paid.
Collected: 130,000 + 5,000 = 135,000 naira. Outstanding: 150,000 minus 135,000 = 15,000 naira (2 x 2,500 from the half payments plus 2 x 5,000 unpaid). She confirms the sheet shows the same figures.

Saved prompt: "Using my context file, write a warm WhatsApp update for our savings group. Collected this month: 135,000 naira of 150,000. Outstanding: 15,000 naira. Next meeting: [date from facts sheet]. Do not name anyone who owes. Under 120 words. Do not calculate or change any figure."
Check: she compares every figure and date in the draft with her sheet and facts sheet, and fixes one sentence where the draft said "most members" instead of "26 of 30 members".
Output: one group message, plus four short private reminders she writes herself to the members who owe, so nobody is shamed in the group.
blocks.result: The routine now takes Funmi about 20 minutes. The AI writes only the words; the sheet does the sums, and her check confirms every figure. Member names, phone numbers and amounts per person never enter the AI tool.

blocks.title: Tell the AI not to touch the figures
blocks.text: Add a line such as "Do not calculate or change any figure" to every prompt that includes numbers, and still check every figure yourself. Assistants sometimes round, reorder or recalculate numbers in a draft.
A research routine with source checks

Research is one of the most useful routines and one of the riskiest, because assistants can state wrong dates, amounts or eligibility rules confidently. The safe pattern is to **research from sources you have chosen**, ask for answers with citations, and then confirm every key fact on the official page yourself.

items: Trigger: first Monday of the month, 30-minute time box.
Inputs: links to official pages of the programmes you follow (government agencies, development partners, your funders), saved in a list in your files.
Add those pages as sources in a NotebookLM notebook, which answers with in-line citations to your sources, or paste the text into your assistant.

Saved prompt: "From these sources only, list each opportunity with: who can apply, deadline, how to apply. Quote the sentence each fact comes from. If a fact is not in the sources, write 'not stated'."
Check: open the official page for every deadline and eligibility rule and confirm it. Delete anything you cannot confirm.
Output: a short brief in your Drive and a summary message to your team, each with the official link.

blocks.title: Opportunity scams
blocks.text: Fake grant, loan and job offers often ask for an "application fee" or "processing fee" paid to a personal account. Treat any request for payment to access a grant as a warning sign, and confirm offers only through the organisation's official website or office.
Your first run

The first run of any routine card is a test. Expect to edit the prompt, add a missing fact to your facts sheet or adjust the time box. Write what went wrong on the card itself. After three runs, most routines settle into a steady shape; if one still needs heavy rewriting each time, the next lesson shows you how to decide whether to fix it or drop it.

takeaways: A routine card answers when, what inputs, which prompt, what check, what output and how long.
The AI works in the middle; you own the inputs, the check and the delivery.
Sums come from a spreadsheet, and prompts say not to change any figure.
Research routines use your chosen sources, citations and a final check on the official page.
Treat the first three runs as tests and edit the card as you learn.

activity.title: Write and run two routine cards
steps: Choose your best first routine from the map in Lesson 1.2 and write its routine card with all eight fields.
Write a second card for a research routine on a topic you follow, listing at least three official source links.
Put both triggers in your calendar as repeating events.
Run each routine once, timing it and noting every edit you made to the draft.
activity.evidence: Photos or files of both routine cards, plus your notes from the first run of each.

lessons.title: Quality gates, the AI work log and a fallback plan
objectives: Set a review gate that matches the risk level of each output
Keep an AI work log and calculate time saved and heavy-edit rate
Apply a clear rule to fix, keep or drop a routine
Write a fallback plan for when a tool or data connection fails

blocks.text: A system that produces fast drafts but lets errors through is worse than no system, because people stop trusting your work. This lesson adds the two parts that keep the system honest: a **review gate** that catches problems before output leaves your hands, and an **AI work log** that shows, with your own figures, which routines are worth keeping.

blocks.name: verify-data
blocks.alt: A person checking data on a screen with a magnifying glass
blocks.caption: Every output passes the review gate before anyone else sees it.

blocks.text: Match the gate to the risk

head: Risk level
Examples
Gate
rows: Low
Your own planning notes, a first list of ideas, an internal draft
Quick read for sense and anything obviously wrong
Medium
Messages to members or clients, reports to your manager, social media posts
Full five-point check below
High
Anything about money, health, legal matters, official statements or a named person's conduct
Five-point check, every claim matched to a source, and a second person reviews; or do it without AI

blocks.title: Five-point check before sending
items: Names and dates match sources
Numbers match the spreadsheet
No private data exposed
Every claim has a source
Sounds like you
blocks.caption: Run these five checks on every medium-risk output; high-risk output also needs a second reviewer.

blocks.text: Check in this order, because the first two catch the most damaging errors. Watch especially for **invented details**: an assistant may add a plausible venue, a speaker's title or a statistic that was never in your inputs. If a sentence contains a fact you did not supply, either confirm it from a reliable source or delete it.

Checking is fastest when you compare the draft with its sources side by side rather than reading it from top to bottom. On a phone, open the sheet or facts sheet in one app and the draft in another, then go through the draft looking only for names, dates and figures, ticking each one. Then read once more for tone. When a second reviewer is needed, send them the draft together with the sources and tell them what to look for, for example "please check the amounts against the attached sheet and confirm nothing private is included". A reviewer who knows what to check catches far more than one asked to "have a look".
The AI work log

Keep one line in a sheet for every routine run, with these columns: date, routine, minutes taken (including checking), estimated minutes without AI (from your before timings), edit level (none, light or heavy), and errors caught. It takes under a minute per run, and after a month it answers the question every manager and client will ask: does this actually help?

blocks.title: Worked example: reading four weeks of log
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi from Lesson 1.1 logged three weekly routines for four weeks: the Monday announcement (40 minutes before), repeat-question replies (60 minutes before) and the roster message (30 minutes before). That is 12 runs in all.
steps: Announcement: 4 runs of 15 minutes = 60 minutes with AI, against 4 x 40 = 160 without. Saved 100 minutes, 25 per run.
Replies: runs of 30, 35, 25 and 30 = 120 minutes, against 4 x 60 = 240. Saved 120 minutes, 30 per run.
Roster: runs of 12, 14, 20 and 14 = 60 minutes, against 4 x 30 = 120. Saved 60 minutes, 15 per run.
Totals: 60 + 120 + 60 = 240 minutes with AI, 160 + 240 + 120 = 520 without. Saved 280 minutes, 4 hours 40 minutes.
Heavy edits: 3 of the 12 runs, which is 25 percent. Errors caught at the gate: 5 (two wrong dates, one wrong name, two invented details).
blocks.result: All three routines pass her keep rule. The five caught errors also show why the gate matters: without it, five mistakes would have reached members. The two wrong dates came from an old facts sheet, so her fix is to update the facts sheet, not the prompt.

blocks.text: A simple keep, fix or drop rule

items: **Keep** a routine that saves at least 10 minutes per run and needs heavy edits in no more than 1 run in 3.
**Fix** a routine that saves time but needs heavy edits often: improve the prompt, add an example or update the facts sheet, then log three more runs.
**Drop** a routine that still saves under 10 minutes per run after fixing, or that keeps producing errors. Doing the task by hand or with a plain template is a valid result.

blocks.text: Your fallback plan

Tools go down, data runs out and accounts get locked. A sound system keeps working at a slower pace. For each routine card, add a fallback line: where the offline template is, which past output you can adapt by hand, and the minimum version you will send if time is short. For example, "If no AI or no data: open last week's announcement offline, change dates from the facts sheet, send."

blocks.title: Monthly system review
blocks.text: On the first working day of each month, spend 20 minutes with your log: total the minutes saved, apply the keep, fix or drop rule, update your facts sheet and context file, and decide whether to add one new routine. One new routine a month is a sustainable pace.

takeaways: Set the review gate by risk: low, medium or high.
The five-point check covers names and dates, numbers, private data, sources and voice.
Log every run; your own figures decide whether a routine stays.
Keep routines that save 10 or more minutes per run with heavy edits in no more than 1 run in 3.
Every routine card needs a fallback for when AI or data is unavailable.

activity.title: Set up your gate and log
steps: Write your five-point check on a card or phone note you can see while working.
Create an AI work log sheet with the six columns from this lesson.
Log every run of your routines for the next four weeks.
At the end, total minutes saved per routine and apply the keep, fix or drop rule.
Add a fallback line to each routine card.
activity.evidence: Your log sheet with at least four weeks of entries and your keep, fix or drop decision for each routine.

quiz.q: Chioma scored Stack B 4, 4, 4, 4 and 3 on criteria weighted 30, 25, 20, 15 and 10. What is its weighted score out of 5?
Funmi's group expects 150,000 naira and collects 135,000. What should her prompt ask the AI to do with these figures?
options: Recalculate them to double-check
Use them exactly as given and not calculate or change any figure
Round them to make the message friendlier
Work out how much each owing member must pay
quiz.explain: The spreadsheet does the sums. The prompt tells the AI to use the figures as given, and Funmi still checks every figure in the draft.

quiz.q: A research routine's AI summary says a grant deadline is 30 November. What should happen before it goes to the team?
options: Send it, since the AI cited a source
Ask the AI again to confirm the date
Remove the date to be safe and send the rest
Open the official page and confirm the deadline yourself
quiz.explain: Every key fact in a research routine is confirmed on the official page before it is shared. Citations make checking faster but do not replace it.

quiz.q: A routine saves 6 minutes per run after two rounds of fixing. Using the course's rule, what should she do?
options: Drop it and use a plain template or do it by hand
Keep it, since any saving counts
Add more AI tools to the routine
Stop logging it
quiz.explain: Routines that still save under 10 minutes per run after fixing are dropped. A plain template or manual method is a valid outcome.

quiz.q: Ngozi's log shows two wrong dates caught at the gate, both from an outdated facts sheet. What is the best fix?
options: Rewrite the prompt
Switch to a different AI tool
Update the facts sheet and set a monthly reminder to review it
Remove dates from all announcements
quiz.explain: The errors came from stale reference facts, so updating the facts sheet fixes the cause. The monthly review keeps it current.

quiz.q: Which output needs a second person's review, or should be done without AI?
options: Your own list of ideas for next month
A weekly roster message
A first draft of your personal to-do list
A statement about a staff member's misconduct
quiz.explain: Outputs about a named person's conduct, money, health, legal or official matters are high risk and need the strictest gate or no AI at all.

modules.title: Coaching Teams, Leading Adoption and Your Portfolio
modules.overview: This module takes your system beyond yourself. You learn to run discovery with a team, price and scope a system-building coaching engagement, lead adoption with a shared team playbook, and present your own measured results as a portfolio case with a 90-day plan.

lessons.title: Discovery: diagnosing how a team really works before adding AI
objectives: Plan a one-week discovery with time diaries, interviews and a look at real work samples
Ask discovery questions that reveal recurring work, risks and readiness
Convert time diary figures into weekly hours per task
Produce a shortlist of first routines with their risks

blocks.text: When a team or small business asks for help "using AI", the request is usually vague. The owner has heard that AI saves time but cannot say where. If you jump straight to training on prompts, people try a few things, nothing sticks and the effort fades. **Discovery** is the short investigation you do first to find out how the work really flows, where time goes, and what the risks are. It turns a vague request into a short, specific plan.

blocks.name: team-collaboration
blocks.alt: A small team discussing work around a board
blocks.caption: Discovery starts with how the team actually works, not with the tools.

blocks.text: A one-week discovery plan

blocks.title: Discovery week
items: Day 1: kickoff with owner
Days 1 to 5: time diaries
Days 3 to 4: role interviews
Day 5: review work samples
Day 6: analyse figures
Day 7: findings meeting
blocks.caption: Time diaries run all week while interviews and sample reviews happen in the middle, so the findings rest on real figures.

items: **Kickoff (Day 1, 45 minutes):** agree the goal, who takes part, what data you may and may not see, and the date of the findings meeting.
**Time diaries (Days 1 to 5):** each person notes recurring tasks and minutes spent, in a simple shared sheet or on paper. Keep it light: task name and minutes only.
**Role interviews (Days 3 to 4, 30 minutes each):** one conversation per role, ideally while they show you the task on their own phone or computer.
**Work samples (Day 5):** look at real reports, message threads and templates, with private details hidden, to see the current quality.
**Analysis (Day 6):** total the diary minutes, map tasks by frequency and judgement, and note risks.
**Findings (Day 7):** present a shortlist of three first routines, each with expected time saved, risks and the check it needs.

blocks.text: Questions that reveal the real work

head: Area
Questions to ask
rows: Recurring work
What do you do every day or every week that feels repetitive? Walk me through the last time you did it. Where do you copy and paste?
Inputs and outputs
Where does the information come from? Who receives the result, and what do they do with it?
Quality and risk
What mistakes have happened in this task before? What would be serious if it went wrong? Does it involve money, customer details or health information?
Readiness
Which phone or computer do you use for this? How do you pay for data? Have you used any AI tool, and how did it go?
Concerns
What worries you about using AI for this? Who must approve changes to how the work is done?

blocks.title: Ask to be shown, not told
blocks.text: People usually describe how a task should work. When they show you on their own device, you see the real version: the copying between apps, the searching through old chats, the workarounds. Those details are where routines save time.

blocks.title: Worked example: discovery at a small dispatch business
blocks.context: For example, Bisi is coaching a six-person delivery and dispatch business in Ibadan that works six days a week. After the discovery week she totals the time diaries.
steps: Delivery status replies to customers on WhatsApp: 2 staff x 75 minutes a day x 6 days = 900 minutes a week.
End-of-day summary for the owner: 1 staff x 40 minutes x 6 days = 240 minutes a week.
Weekly payment reminders to business customers: 90 minutes a week.
Total: 900 + 240 + 90 = 1,230 minutes, which is 20.5 hours a week across these three tasks.

Risk notes: status replies contain customer names and addresses, so the routine must use saved reply templates and an AI-drafted FAQ rather than pasting customer details into a chatbot. The payment reminders involve money, so amounts come from the accounts sheet and the owner approves the wording once.
blocks.result: Bisi's findings shortlist three routines: a reviewed library of status reply templates drafted with AI, an end-of-day summary built from a shared sheet, and a payment reminder template with figures filled from the accounts sheet. Each has an expected saving to test, a named owner and a check.

blocks.text: Readiness and honesty

Discovery sometimes shows that AI is not the first fix. If the team has no shared sheet, uses five different WhatsApp groups for the same customers, or nobody knows the current prices, a simple template or a tidy-up will save more time than any AI routine. Say so plainly in your findings. Clients trust advisers who recommend the cheapest thing that works.

Present findings in a short meeting, not a long document. Show the diary totals first, because owners are often surprised by where the hours really go. Then show the three proposed routines, the risk and check for each, and what you will measure. End by asking the owner to choose a start date and name an owner for each routine. A findings meeting that ends without names and dates usually leads nowhere.

blocks.title: Handle discovery data with care
blocks.text: Time diaries and work samples can contain customer and staff details. Agree at kickoff what you will see, ask for private details to be hidden in samples, store notes in a protected folder, and delete copies you no longer need when the work ends.

takeaways: Discovery turns a vague request for AI help into a specific, measured plan.
Use time diaries, role interviews and real work samples over about one week.
Ask to be shown the task on the person's own device.
Convert diary minutes into weekly hours to find where time really goes.
Recommend non-AI fixes when they are simpler and cheaper.

activity.title: Run a mini discovery
steps: Find one colleague, friend or small business owner willing to help.
Ask them to keep a three-day time diary of recurring tasks with minutes.
Hold a 30-minute interview using at least six questions from the table.
Total the minutes per task and convert to hours per week.
Write a one-page shortlist of two first routines, with risks and checks.
activity.evidence: The time diary totals and your one-page shortlist (with private details removed).

lessons.title: Pricing and scoping a system-building coaching engagement
objectives: Compare a one-off workshop with a multi-week build-and-coach engagement
Estimate hours for each stage and calculate a fee with contingency
Write in-scope and out-of-scope lists and a change request rule
Set clear terms on accounts, subscriptions and client data

blocks.text: Helping others build AI productivity systems can become paid work for a consultant or coach, or an internal service you offer as a team lead. Either way, clear scope and honest pricing protect both sides. The key fact about this work is that **habits take weeks to form**. A single training day teaches ideas, but the routines usually need follow-up to stick.

blocks.name: handshake
blocks.caption: A clear agreement on scope and fees protects you and your client.

blocks.text: Two common offers

blocks.title: Workshop or build-and-coach
items: One-off workshop
Six-week build-and-coach
right: Higher fee, more of your time
blocks.caption: A workshop suits teams that only need the ideas; build-and-coach suits teams that want working routines and evidence.

blocks.text: Costing by stages

Estimate your hours for each stage, multiply by your hourly rate, then add **contingency** (an allowance for things taking longer than planned) of about 10 to 20 percent. Set your rate from your experience, what similar services in your area charge, and what the client can afford. Do not copy a rate from someone else's course or social media post without checking it against your local market.

Track your real hours on your first two or three engagements, stage by stage. Most people underestimate preparation, travel and follow-up messages. Your own records will make each later estimate more accurate, and they help you explain your fee calmly if a client questions it.

blocks.title: Worked example: costing a six-week engagement
blocks.context: For example, Bisi prices the dispatch business engagement from Lesson 3.1. She uses an illustrative rate of 10,000 naira an hour; this is a figure for practice, not a market rate.
steps: Discovery week: 8 hours.
Designing and building the context file, three routine cards and templates: 10 hours.
Training session with the team: 3 hours.
Weekly check-ins: 6 x 1 hour = 6 hours, plus preparation and follow-up notes: 6 x 0.5 = 3 hours.
Final review of the log and handover: 3 hours.
Contingency of 15 percent: 330,000 x 1.15 = 379,500 naira, rounded to 380,000 naira. Payment: 50 percent (190,000 naira) on signing, 50 percent on handover.
blocks.result: Bisi's proposal shows the stages and hours, so the owner can see what the fee buys. If the owner wants a lower price, Bisi removes a stage (for example, three check-ins instead of six) rather than cutting her rate.

blocks.text: Scope: in, out and changes

head: In scope
Out of scope
rows: Discovery week and written findings
Building automations between apps or custom software
Context file, up to three routine cards and templates
Writing the team's daily messages for them
One training session and six weekly check-ins
Paying for AI subscriptions or data
Log template and final results review
Handling customer personal data on the client's behalf

blocks.text: Add a **change request rule**: any new routine, extra training session or additional team member is quoted separately and agreed in writing before work starts. A WhatsApp message saying "Yes, agreed" from the owner is better than nothing; a short signed note is better still.
Writing the proposal

items: Summary: the client's goal in their own words, taken from your discovery findings.
Approach: the stages, what happens in each and who from the team must take part.
Deliverables: the context file, routine cards, templates, log and final review, listed one per line.
Timeline: start date, check-in day of the week and handover date.
Fee and payment: the costing table, contingency, total, payment dates and receipts.
Scope and terms: in scope, out of scope, change request rule and data rules.

blocks.text: If you lead a team inside an organisation rather than selling to clients, the same proposal still helps. Replace the fee with the staff hours you are asking for, and get your manager's written agreement on the scope and data rules before you start. Internal work without an agreed scope tends to grow until it stalls.
Terms that prevent later disputes

items: **The client owns the accounts.** AI tools, Drive folders and subscriptions are created in the client's name, so nothing breaks when you leave.
**Data rules in writing.** List what may go into AI tools (templates, anonymised examples) and what may not (customer details, staff records, payment information).
**Results are estimates.** Promise to measure, not a fixed number of hours saved. The log will show the real figure.
**Payment terms.** State amounts, dates and the account for payment, and issue a receipt for every payment.

blocks.title: Do not oversell
blocks.text: Avoid promises like "double your productivity" or "save 20 hours a week". You do not yet know, and the client will remember. Offer to measure before and after, and let your log speak in the final review.

takeaways: Routines take weeks to stick, so build-and-coach often delivers more than a single workshop.
Cost by stage: hours x rate, plus 10 to 20 percent contingency.
Lower the price by removing stages, not by cutting your rate.
Write in-scope, out-of-scope and change request terms.
The client owns accounts and data rules are agreed in writing.

activity.title: Draft a one-page proposal
steps: Choose either a workshop or a six-week build-and-coach offer for the person from your mini discovery.
List the stages and estimate hours for each.
Calculate the fee with your own hourly rate and a contingency between 10 and 20 percent; check the sums with a calculator or sheet.
Write in-scope and out-of-scope lists, a change request rule and the four terms.
Ask a friend to read it and tell you anything that is unclear.
activity.evidence: Your one-page proposal with the costing table and scope lists.

lessons.title: Leading team adoption, building your portfolio and a 90-day plan
objectives: Create a team AI playbook with shared context, prompts, routine owners and rules
Measure adoption with a routine run rate
Write an honest portfolio case study with measured results
Draft a 90-day plan for your own system or coaching work

blocks.text: A personal system depends on one person. A team system must survive holidays, staff changes and busy seasons. That needs a shared, written **team AI playbook** and someone who leads adoption by example, not by announcement.

blocks.name: progress-tracking
blocks.alt: A person reviewing progress bars on a dashboard
blocks.caption: Leading adoption means tracking whether routines actually run, week after week.

blocks.text: The team AI playbook

items: **Shared context file and facts sheet:** one version, with a named person responsible for updates and a date at the top.
**Prompt library:** tested prompts for each routine, numbered, with the date last tested.
**Routine cards with owners:** every routine has one named owner and one backup.
**Approved tools list:** which AI tools may be used for work, and with which accounts.
**AI use rules:** what never goes into AI tools, which outputs need a second reviewer, and how to label AI-assisted documents if your organisation requires it.
**Review rhythm:** a 20-minute monthly look at the log, owned by the team lead.

blocks.title: Champions, not commands
blocks.text: Pick one willing person per team as a routine champion. They run the routine visibly, help colleagues in the first weeks and report problems early. People adopt what they see a trusted colleague using successfully.
Handling worries and resistance

Some colleagues will be keen and some will hold back. Common worries are that AI will make mistakes in their name, that their job is at risk, or that they will look foolish while learning. Take each worry seriously. Point to the review gate: nothing leaves without a human check, and the person who sends it owns it. Explain that routines remove repetitive steps so people have more time for the work only they can do, such as customer relationships and judgement calls. Offer private practice time before anyone is expected to use a routine in front of others.

Watch the opposite risk too. Enthusiastic users sometimes skip the check because the drafts usually look right. A short monthly look at the log, including errors caught, keeps everyone honest without blaming anyone.
Measuring adoption

Time saved matters, but first you need to know whether routines are actually being run. The **run rate** is the number of routine runs completed divided by the number scheduled. A low run rate tells you the routine is too hard, poorly timed or not understood, and that problem must be fixed before measuring savings.

blocks.title: Worked example: six weeks of adoption at the dispatch business
blocks.context: For example, after Bisi's engagement the dispatch business ran three routines for six weeks, working six days a week.
steps: Daily status replies drafted from the template library: scheduled 6 days x 6 weeks = 36 runs; completed 30.
Weekly summary report to the owner, built from the daily sheet: scheduled 6, completed 6.
Weekly payment reminders: scheduled 6, completed 4.
Total: 36 + 6 + 6 = 48 scheduled; 30 + 6 + 4 = 40 completed. Run rate: 40 / 48 = 83 percent.
The payment reminder routine is lowest at 4 of 6. In the review, staff explain it falls on Saturday, their busiest day. The owner moves the trigger to Thursday.
blocks.result: An 83 percent run rate shows the routines are mostly in use, and the one weak routine has a clear, simple fix. Bisi records the run rate, the minutes saved from the log and the change made as evidence for her portfolio, with the owner's permission.

blocks.text: An honest portfolio case study

Whether you want a promotion, a coaching client or a new job, evidence beats claims. One well-documented case is worth more than a list of tools you have used. Write it in five short parts, and include what did not work: it shows judgement and makes the rest believable.

items: **Starting point:** the task, who did it, and the before timings.
**What you built:** the context store, routine cards and checks, with a screenshot of one routine card (private details hidden).
**Measured result:** minutes saved from the log, run rate, errors caught at the gate.
**What did not work:** a routine you dropped or fixed, and why.
**What changed next:** the decision or improvement that followed.

blocks.title: Permission and privacy
blocks.text: Ask the client or your manager before naming them or sharing any figures from their work, and remove customer and staff details from screenshots. If they prefer, describe the case without the organisation's name, for example "a six-person dispatch business in Ibadan".
Your 90-day plan

blocks.title: 90-day plan
items: Days 1 to 30: run and log
Days 31 to 60: pilot with one person
Days 61 to 90: case study and offer
blocks.caption: Prove the system on yourself first, then help one other person, then package the evidence.

items: **Days 1 to 30:** run at least two routines from your own system, log every run and complete one monthly review.
**Days 31 to 60:** help one colleague, friend or small business build one routine, using a short discovery and a routine card. Agree to log results together.
**Days 61 to 90:** write your own case study and, if you want paid work, a one-page offer and proposal based on Lesson 3.2. Share it with three people who could use or refer the service.

takeaways: A team playbook holds shared context, tested prompts, routine owners, approved tools and rules.
Run rate (completed runs divided by scheduled runs) shows whether routines are really used.
Fix low run rates before measuring time saved.
A strong case study includes before figures, what you built, measured results and what did not work.
Prove the system on yourself, then one other person, then package the evidence.

activity.title: Draft your playbook page and 90-day plan
steps: Write a one-page playbook for your own work or team using the six headings.
Calculate the run rate for your routines from your log so far.
Draft the five-part case study outline with the figures you have.
Write your 90-day plan with one measurable target for each 30-day block.
activity.evidence: Your playbook page, run rate calculation, case study outline and 90-day plan.

quiz.q: Bisi's diaries show 2 staff each spend 75 minutes a day on status replies, 6 days a week. How many hours a week is that?
options: 9 hours
12.5 hours
15 hours
20.5 hours
quiz.explain: 2 x 75 x 6 = 900 minutes, and 900 divided by 60 is 15 hours. 20.5 hours is the total for all three tasks.

quiz.q: During discovery, a staff member describes how a task should work. What gives you a more accurate picture?
options: Asking the owner instead
Asking them to show you the last time they did it on their own device
Reading an online article about the industry
Asking an AI tool how such businesses work
quiz.explain: Being shown the real task reveals the copying, searching and workarounds where routines save time.

quiz.q: A proposal totals 33 hours at an illustrative 10,000 naira an hour with 15 percent contingency. What is the fee before rounding?
options: 330,000 naira
345,000 naira
363,000 naira
379,500 naira

quiz.q: A client says the fee is too high. What does the course recommend?
options: Remove a stage, such as fewer check-ins, and keep your rate
Cut your hourly rate in half
Promise a guaranteed number of hours saved
Drop the contingency and the data rules
quiz.explain: Reducing scope keeps the price honest and protects the value of your time. Guarantees of hours saved are a form of overselling.

quiz.q: Three routines were scheduled 48 times in six weeks and completed 40 times. What is the run rate, and what does a low rate on one routine suggest?
options: 40 percent; the AI tool is weak
83 percent; that routine may be too hard or badly timed
120 percent; the team is over-performing
48 percent; the team needs more AI tools
quiz.explain: 40 divided by 48 is about 83 percent. A routine that is rarely run usually has a timing or difficulty problem, like the Saturday payment reminders.

quiz.q: Which belongs in an honest portfolio case study?
options: Only the routines that worked
A promise of future savings
The client's customer list as proof
A routine you dropped and why
quiz.explain: Including what did not work shows judgement and makes the measured results believable. Customer details must never be shared.

finalQuiz.q: What best describes an AI productivity system?
options: Using the most advanced AI app available
Habits, files and checks that make AI part of recurring work, with review and measurement
Letting AI handle all tasks automatically
Asking AI questions whenever you remember
finalQuiz.explain: A system combines capture, a context store, routines, a review gate and a log. The tool alone is not the system.

finalQuiz.q: A 15-minute task is done on about 22 working days a month. How many minutes a month does it cost?
options: 150 minutes
220 minutes
330 minutes
37 minutes
finalQuiz.explain: 15 x 22 = 330 minutes a month, more than many monthly tasks that feel bigger.

finalQuiz.q: Which step should be a 'Tool or template' step rather than an AI step?
options: Totalling member contributions for the month
Turning bullet notes into a friendly message
Suggesting a simpler wording for a paragraph
Deciding which member gets support first
finalQuiz.explain: Totals belong in a spreadsheet formula. Drafting and rewording suit AI; deciding priorities needs your judgement.

finalQuiz.q: Which layer of the context store shows the AI what good output looks like?
options: Reference facts
The context file
The calendar trigger
Examples of past good work
finalQuiz.explain: Two or three past outputs you were proud of show the AI the target, often better than a description.

finalQuiz.q: On a free ChatGPT plan, OpenAI's help page gives custom instructions a limit of how many characters?
options: No limit
finalQuiz.explain: The help page lists up to 1,500 characters on Free and Go plans and up to 5,000 on paid plans. Check the page, as limits can change.

finalQuiz.q: Which habit reduces data costs when using AI on a phone?
options: Using voice conversations for every task
Uploading large recordings on mobile data
Typing text chats and uploading big files on Wi-Fi
Opening the app many times a day for single questions
finalQuiz.explain: Text uses far less data than voice, images or video, and large uploads are better done on Wi-Fi. Batching routines also helps.

finalQuiz.q: A routine card has a trigger, inputs, saved prompt, check, output, time box and log. What is the trigger?
options: The fixed time or event that starts the routine
The AI tool used
The person who receives the output
The error the check catches
finalQuiz.explain: The trigger, such as 'last Friday of the month at 7pm', makes the routine happen even in a busy week.

finalQuiz.q: A research routine's summary includes a deadline that is not in any of your chosen sources. What should you do?
options: Keep it, since AI tools are usually right
Change it to a later date to be safe
Ask the AI to rephrase it
Delete it unless you can confirm it on the official page
finalQuiz.explain: Facts not found in your sources may be invented. Confirm on the official page or remove them.

finalQuiz.q: Over four weeks, routines took 240 minutes with AI against an estimated 520 without. How much time was saved?
options: 280 minutes, 4 hours 40 minutes
240 minutes, 4 hours
760 minutes, about 12.7 hours
520 minutes, about 8.7 hours
finalQuiz.explain: 520 minus 240 = 280 minutes, which is 4 hours 40 minutes. Checking time is included in the 240.

finalQuiz.q: During discovery at a business, you find staff use five WhatsApp groups for the same customers and have no shared price list. What should your findings say?
options: Buy paid AI subscriptions for everyone
Fix the shared price list and channels first, since that may save more than any AI routine
Train staff on advanced prompts immediately
Leave it out, since the client asked about AI
finalQuiz.explain: Good advisers recommend the simplest fix that works, even when it is not AI. Clients trust that honesty.

finalQuiz.q: Which term protects both sides in a coaching engagement?
options: The coach owns the client's AI accounts
A guaranteed saving of 20 hours a week
Customer data shared freely to speed up the work
The client owns accounts, and data rules are agreed in writing
finalQuiz.explain: Client-owned accounts keep the system working after you leave, and written data rules prevent misuse of personal information.

finalQuiz.q: In the team playbook, why does every routine have a named owner and a backup?
options: So the routine keeps running during leave or staff changes
So the AI knows who to blame
So more people can use the paid plan
So the run rate can be above 100 percent
finalQuiz.explain: A team system must survive holidays and staff changes. An owner and a backup keep each routine running.

capstone.title: Personal AI Productivity System Project
capstone.brief: Build, run and evaluate your own AI productivity system for at least four weeks, then present it as a measured case study with a 90-day plan for refining it or offering system-building coaching.
steps: Complete a two-week recurring task inventory with minutes per month, and break your top three tasks into steps with the four roles.
Build your context store: a context file within your tool's limit, one template, two examples and a dated facts sheet.
Write at least two routine cards (one may be a research routine) with triggers, checks and fallbacks, and put the triggers in your calendar.
Run the routines for at least four weeks, passing every output through the review gate and logging each run.
Apply the keep, fix or drop rule, and write a five-part case study with your before and after figures and what did not work.
Write a 90-day plan with one measurable target per 30-day block.
evidence: Task inventory and step-role table for three tasks
Context file with character count and a screenshot of the context store folder
Two routine cards with fallback lines
AI work log covering at least four weeks, with totals and keep, fix or drop decisions
Five-part case study with private details removed
